records.title: EHRs: What to Know, When to Start, How to Get Beyond the Challenges
records.abstract: With the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA) designating $17 billion in financial incentives for physicians and hospitals to adopt electronic health records (EHRs) over the next five years, more and more oncologists and cancer centers will be making the switch from paper-based records. And while making the transition can be challenging, the technology does have many benefits, including ready access to patient information, automated chemotherapy ordering, improved quality control and enhanced efficiency, and opportunities for clinical data analysis. This first article in our three-part series details those benefits. Part 2 will look at the challenges, and Part 3 will discuss the details of what to look for in a good EHR system. One of the advantages of an EHR system, obviously, is the ability to readily access patient records: “Oncology is a data-driven business,” said Lynn H. Vogel, PhD, Vice President and Chief Information Officer of the University of Texas M. D. Anderson Cancer Center. Laboratory and pathology results and radiology images are all basic tools in reaching diagnosis and developing treatment regimens, said Dr. Vogel, who is also Associate Professor in M. D. Anderson's Department of Bioinformatics and Computational Biology. ClinicStation—The Center's EHR system, which has evolved in-house over the last 10 years—makes it possible for physicians to have access to all of this data, whether they are in their office, at the patient's bedside, at home, or traveling.Figure: LYNN H. VOGEL, PHD: “If you consider our 700 to 800 physicians [at M. D. Anderson] and put in basic assumptions about salaries, we can pretty easily assume that we're saving about $15 million a year just from that one feature alone.”Being able to view patient records anywhere is one of the biggest benefits of using an EHR, agreed Douglas W. Blayney, MD, Medical Director of the University of Michigan Comprehensive Cancer Center (UMCCC) and President of the American Society of Clinical Oncology. The UMCCC's EHR system is a home-built document viewer, or picture archiver and communications (PAC) system, and allows physicians to see patient notes, prescriptions, recently administered chemotherapy, lab and pathology reports, and images of x-rays and other scans, Dr. Blayney explained. “The other advantage is that I can easily share these documents across our continuum of care, whether it's with a primary care office or consultants such as surgeons, pulmonologists, or emergency room physicians.” Ordering Chemotherapy EHR systems also have the potential to be tailored to oncology-specific needs such as chemotherapy ordering—“the most distinct functionality that sets oncology apart from other areas of medicine,” said John V. Cox, DO, Immediate Past Chair of ASCO's EHR Workgroup and a specialist in hematology and medical oncology at Texas Oncology Methodist Cancer Centers in Houston. The EHR system at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute contains chemotherapy ordering as well as infusion flow sheets and tumor staging. “Dana-Farber developed its first EHR modules according to area of risk,” explained Lawrence N. Shulman, MD, Chief Medical Officer, Senior Vice President for Medical Affairs, and Chief of the Division of General Oncology there. Consequently, parenteral chemotherapy ordering was one of the first systems to become electronic in the 1990s and has been updated based on improving technologies and safety features. In June, Dana-Farber added an ordering system for oral chemotherapies such as capecitabine and lapatinib to its EHR, using many of the safety features in the parenteral chemotherapy modules to ensure patient safety, Dr. Shulman noted. Improvements in Quality Control & Efficiency Dana-Farber also uses EHRs to assess quality standards for its practice. The chemotherapy ordering, for example, is guideline driven—after a patient receives a diagnosis, the EHR calls up a set of acceptable chemotherapy regimens. Guideline adherence is measured as a quality standard and is one of the center's pay-for-performance measures with Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts.Figure: MICHAEL BOOKMAN, MD: “It's clear that staff can perform more efficiently and that EHR increases patient volume. We also have the potential to reduce medical errors, which provides a cost savings at multiple levels.”The institute's EHR also alerts physicians about patient allergies to medications. “We don't want an allergy to completely prevent the administration of a drug, because there are cases where a hypersensitivity reaction can be managed,” Dr. Shulman said. “But providers should know it's an issue so they can give the appropriate premedication.” At Fox Chase Cancer Center, quality control has just recently become part of the EHR system, noted Michael Bookman, MD, Vice President of Ambulatory Care and Clinical Research. Using integrated rules-based workflow capability in the EHR software Soarian, physicians can be alerted if a patient's weight changes before undergoing chemotherapy, for example. Quality control alerts are particularly useful for drug utilization-associated toxicities, since keeping an eye on what drugs oncologists are prescribing and how these may interact with other medications the patient is taking can be difficult for any one person to do. Similar quality-control measures are integrated into the EHR at the Cleveland Clinic's Taussig Cancer Institute, where, for example, the system requires the intake nurse who is seeing patients for the first time to ask about fertility and whether they want children. The answer can affect how chemotherapy is administered, noted Derek Raghavan, MD, PhD, Taussig's Chair and Director. An electronic health record also cuts down on paperwork, freeing up time to spend with patients, said Rajiv Datta, MD, Medical Director of the South Nassau Cancer Center and Chairman of the Department of Surgery and Director of Surgical Oncology at South Nassau Communities Hospital in Oceanside, NY. EHRs also cut down on the time spent making decisions, because patient records are much more accessible, he said. EHRs are also more legible and easier to reproduce compared with handwritten files, Dr. Raghavan noted. The Cleveland Clinic's EHR allows for much faster transcription than paper-based systems because physicians can either type or dictate notes. Improvements in efficiency resulting from EHR implementation, though, are difficult to measure, said Judy Smith, MD, Medical Director and Associate Professor of Oncology at Roswell Park Cancer Institute (RPCI). “Part of what you do when you implement an EHR is look at different work flows and processes and try to improve them. A lot of beneficial changes are due to adjustments made to workflow and are not necessarily inherent in EHR. It's hard to determine which component is the driver of excellence.”Figure: LAWRENCE N. SHULMAN, MD: “If I spend 20% of my time on a task in a paper-based setting and 15% on the same task with EHR, I'm saving 5% of my time, but this is hard to translate into dollar savings.”The EHR system Eclipsys, implemented more than six years ago at RPCI, has helped to cut down on patient errors and has made transcription easier, she said. The EHR system also searches for and eliminates duplicate orders and tests. Clinical Data Analysis EHRs also have the potential for use in analyzing clinical data, Dr. Smith noted: Opportunities exist for using EHR at Roswell Park to pursue clinical and quality research by evaluating data in the aggregate. Additionally, the clinical research team uses the EHR system to alert practitioners about their patients' protocol eligibility. Fox Chase uses its EHR to track patient data for the approximately 170 clinical trials being conducted at any time, Dr. Bookman said. The center had to develop a custom system because of the highly regulated nature of how patients need to be managed in clinical trials. An EHR system can also facilitate chart reviews for research and quality-of-care efforts, Dr. Blayney said. “We do a lot of chart reviews, so it's nice not having to chase down paper.” And Dr. Vogel noted that to manage M. D. Anderson's research data sets, the cancer center is currently implementing a product called ResearchStation, built on the same services-oriented architecture as the ClinicStation EHR system, making, therefore, data from the clinical encounter and data from research processes interoperable. Measuring Cost Savings While the transition to an electronic health record likely saves institutions money, measuring these savings is difficult, those interviewed for this article agreed. While no formal data exist, “it's clear that staff can perform more efficiently and that EHR increases patient volume,” Dr. Bookman said. “We also have the potential to reduce medical errors, which saves money at multiple levels.” Another measure of cost savings is evaluating how much money was needed to store, file, and retrieve paper records before EHR was implemented, Dr. Shulman said. The cost of EHR, including startup, training and user fees, and money spent on ongoing maintenance, also needs to be considered. He estimated that Dana-Farber has probably saved hundreds of thousands of dollars in transcription costs, filing paper records, and retrieving charts, but actual numbers are not available. Workflow efficiency should be evaluated as well, Dr. Shulman said. “If I spend 20% of my time on a task in a paper-based setting and 15% on the same task with EHR, I'm saving 5% of my time, but this is hard to translate into dollar savings.” Dr. Vogel pointed out that another cost saver to consider is ready access to radiology films, since physicians no longer have to ask someone to go to the film lab and pull an image. Eliminating this process and giving physicians simultaneous electronic access to films for consultation purposes has had an enormous impact on cost savings and quality of care, he said. At M. D. Anderson, physicians report that EHR easily saves them a half hour a day in finding medical records and getting lab results, Dr. Vogel said. “If you consider our 700 to 800 physicians and put in basic assumptions about salaries, we can pretty easily assume that we're saving about $15 million a year just from that one feature.” ASCO EHR Symposium in October The American Society of Clinical Oncology's Second EHR Symposium: Harnessing the EHR, from Incentives to Sustainability, will be held October 6-7 in San Francisco (http://tinyurl.com/ASCO-EHRSymposium). Involving Patients in EHR Management To enhance their EHR systems, many facilities are developing communication tools to help patients fill out necessary forms and access their medical information. Lynn H. Vogel, PhD, Vice President and Chief Information Officer at M. D. Anderson Cancer Center, notes that the center has recently implemented myMDAnderson, a Web portal that allows patients to access their medical record information. The site also enables referring physicians to view their patients' complete EHR records. At Fox Chase Cancer Center, a new initiative involves self-service kiosks at the clinic, which allow patients to update their insurance information, pay bills, and access consent forms, said Michael Bookman, MD, Vice President of Ambulatory Care and Clinical Research. The kiosk also gives patients a printed itinerary of their appointments and tracks them during their visit. And at the Cleveland Clinic's Taussig Cancer Institute, patients can view portions of their medical record via a Web-based system called MyChart. Patients can also request and cancel appointments and ask for prescription renewals. Moreover, noted Taussig Chair and Director Derek Raghavan, MD, PhD, the system also offers patients reminders about routine lab procedures such as cholesterol tests and provides them with information on how to stop smoking.

records.title: Editors’ Choice
records.venue: BJOG An International Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology
records.abstract: I am writing my editor’s choice from the maternity hospital at Bwaila in Lilongwe, Malawi. Between 15 000 and 16 000 babies are born here each year and the understaffed unit (only one obstetric consultant) fight valiantly each day to reverse the ever surging tide of obstructed labour. Obstructed labour, when prolonged, results in an array of acute problems such as uterine rupture (of which we have repaired many during my 10 days here) and postpartum haemorrhage, and the chronic sequelae include obstetric fistulae. My colleague, Jeff Wilkinson (who directs the Freedom from Fistula Foundation [University of North Carolina] unit here) and I have just finished repair of a vesicovaginal fistula transvaginally and a uterovesicovaginal fistula transabdominally with reimplantation of the ureter. These complex cases abound in a country where access to safe and timely abdominal delivery is limited. Our medical colleagues have done much better in addressing the problem of HIV infection. Their success has been in part because they are delivering a relatively simple therapy rather than complex surgery, and also in part because of the commitment of the developed world to invest in making these therapies available. This makes a death from postpartum haemorrhage with a viral load at zero a particularly tragic loss. Rodriguez et al., in their intriguing decision analytic models on page 1067, mathematically simulate what would happen if injectable progestin contraception, which may be associated with an increased propensity to acquire HIV, was no longer used in Chad, Kenya, South Africa and Uganda. As a result of the 1 in 32 lifetime risk of maternal death from pregnancy in these countries, loss of this effective form of contraception would result in nine additional maternal deaths for each case of HIV averted. Their work not only demonstrates the importance of contraception in countries where childbirth is unsafe, it re-emphasises the huge potential to save lives that making abdominal deliveries readily available could have. This will be far more difficult to achieve than ensuring the delivery of a pharmacological intervention (which does not decry the importance, or underestimate the difficulty, of introducing effective drug treatments for infectious disease). Gupta et al. on page 1058, in a cross-sectional study from Cote d’Ivoire show the critical role of mothers-in-law in women’s health. They surveyed women of reproductive age (with an impressive 96% response rate) and found that mothers-in-law—either through verbal or physical violence—have a profound influence on the timing of pregnancy, family size and contraception. I did my own informal survey on-site here in Malawi and had this confirmed (‘mothers-in-law will encourage their sons to take another wife if a new bride is not pregnant within a year’). Moreover, the influence of a husband’s mother extends into pregnancy and labour. With respect to village marriages in Malawi, the mother-in-law confirms the diagnosis of pregnancy, establishes the due date (despite last menstrual periods being an inaccurate mechanism), and determines when someone should go to the hospital in labour. Caesarean sections are seen as evidence of a ‘lazy’ or ‘unfaithful’ wife and many mothers-in-law advocate polygamy if such is needed. Before one becomes too outraged at these grandmothers, please keep in mind that in Malawi social security payments, pensions and welfare do not exist and grandchildren are seen as the best hope for care in one’s old age. This important paper allows BJOG readers to learn how entrenched the patrilineal bias is in African culture and how important the education and empowerment of women is for any solution proposed to reduce maternal mortality. My oldest son, a budding biostatistician, called me early in an on-call shift because he was trying to hastily complete an assignment that required a brief concept proposal (as if one were writing a grant application). I suggested my favourite topic, preterm birth (PTB) and next heard from him around 4:00 a.m. He informed me that the research on PTB was suboptimal, confidence intervals were wide, and that most of the things we call risk factors were not modifiable (it is for such insights that I am willing to pay his tuition fees). Myung et al. on page 1029 address in their systematic review one of the few potentially modifiable risk factors for PTB—cigarette smoking. Unlike race, parity, previous preterm birth, or abnormal placentation, women can alter their smoking habits. More importantly, smoking cessation seems to mitigate the increased risk. The difficulty is that tobacco addiction is notoriously difficult to treat. Myung et al.’s meta-analysis documents the effectiveness of various forms of pharmacotherapy and demonstrates that none are clearly superior. Their study is underpowered to assess safety, although there was no evidence that any of the techniques were unsafe. Before any clinician becomes too excited, please note that the mean abstinence rate associated with pharmacotherapy was only 13%. That highlights the difficult fact that most smokers who are going to stop, stop as soon as pregnancy is confirmed and long before encountering health care. Those who continue to smoke are highly addicted to nicotine and recalcitrant to counselling and drugs. Perhaps smoking is not the modifiable risk factor we all think it is. The twentieth century saw a profound shift in the site of childbirth from home to hospital, which occurred as part of the ‘medicalisation of pregnancy’. Although this was associated with dramatic decreases in maternal mortality (think of the high maternal mortality in Africa, where such a shift has not yet happened in most places), many clinicians and mothers have questioned whether less medical settings can be suitable for some women. Inherent in this question is the presumption that women at low risk for medical intervention can be identified reliably and given this option. Rowe et al. on page 1081, in a population-based, cohort study from the UK report on women delivering at freestanding midwifery units, comparing them with those situated alongside hospital units, and identifying women who were transferred to hospital care. Of the 29 248 labours studied, around one in four women needed transfer (21% in alongside units and 27% in freestanding units). Nulliparity was the most important factor associated with transfer and failure to progress was the leading diagnosis. The main difference between groups was that in the alongside units, 14.9% of those transferred did so because they wanted epidural anaesthesia, compared with only 6.1% of those in the freestanding units. Presumably the ease of transfer associated with proximity was an important influence in these cases, whereas the greater distance from the hospital of freestanding units prompted the midwives to recommend earlier transfer in women with slow labour. These data should be informative for women and clinicians making decisions about where to have their babies. As Africa becomes more developed, and women become better educated and so more empowered, one might assume that the influence of mothers-in-law would decrease and that young women would follow their Western sisters and delay childbearing. A good example of such an evolution is Norway, where between 1978 and 2009 the mean maternal age increased from 23 to 28 years of age. With increasing age come reproductive problems, some of which seem to be universal, such as declines in fecundity and increases in aneuploidy and dystocia, and others are selective (affecting only a subset of women) such as insulin resistance and hypertension. On page 1108 Aasheim et al. show that in terms of mood disorders, advancing age seems to be associated with depression only in women with a past history of that problem. This was the case up until 18 months postpartum and should be reassuring to women and their clinicians. Epidemiologists can continue to bow and pay homage to the Scandinavian perinatal cohorts, which have done so much to advance our knowledge. In February’s issue, Makgoba et al. highlighted the differences in the incidence of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) between racial groups, with both African and South Asian origin older mothers in the UK having much higher rates of GDM than white European women of the same age (Makgoba et al. BJOG 2012;119:276–82). In this month’s issue, on page 1091, the same authors present their analysis of the effect of GDM on birthweight. Their most striking finding is the key influence of maternal body mass index (BMI). The higher incidence of larger babies associated with GDM can be largely mitigated by having a low normal BMI. But we all know that the ‘problem of obesity is getting bigger’. How can this be countered? On page 1098, Oostdam et al. report on their randomised controlled trial of the effectiveness of an exercise programme for overweight or obese pregnant women at risk for GDM. Sadly, there were no effects on fasting blood glucose, insulin sensitivity and birthweight, because of poor compliance with the exercise regimen. One can hypothesise that in evolutionary terms, the limited food supply available to our ancestors promoted only the exercise needed for essential activities such as food finding and procreation, ‘rest and relaxation’ being the order of the day to conserve resources when these essential tasks had been completed. So promoting exercise not related to work or reproduction is an uphill struggle, and innovative as yet undiscovered strategies will be needed (which will probably seem obvious in retrospect, as is often the case with lateral thinking solutions). Shakila Thangaratinam’s thoughtful mini-commentary (page 1107) attached to this paper describes her recently published meta-analyses, which show that dietary interventions are more successful than encouraging exercise during pregnancy. Even more valuable would be a strategy to persuade women to optimise their weight (and general health) before conceiving. However, a recent audit of a regional programme of preconception counselling in the UK showed that 73% of women with diabetes had not received any such care (Murphy et al. Diabetes Care 2010;33:2514–20). This probably means that to be effective, a general educational health strategy would have to be implemented in schools. The introduction of education about healthy lifestyles and preparations for parenting in secondary schools is now supported by the Public Health Agency of Canada (www.phac-aspc.gc.ca/hp-ps/dca-dea/publications/fcm-smp/fcmc-smpf-03-eng.php#school). However, we are likely to have to struggle against the commercial might of the fast food industry and resist, for example, the use of vending machines full of calories as income generators for schools (www.guardian.co.uk/education/2012/may/14/academies-sell-banned-junk-food). The responsibility of the medical profession cannot end at the hospital doors.▮

records.title: Freedom of Choice and Fair Share of Burden in a Depopulated Society
records.abstract: “Gender equality will raise the total fertility rate (TFR).” This is the most dominant discourse on fertility these days. In this paper, I criticize such discourses and statistics, using research literacy methods.First of all, according to an international comparison among OECD countries, there seems to be a strong positive correlation coefficient between the rate of female labor participation, the amount of public expenditure toward children, and TFR. The samples are, however, often selected in some arbitrary ways. In fact, there is no correlation.Secondly, based on JGSS2001 data, I find that the sharing of domestic labor by husbands cannot increase the number of children. Thirdly, “gender equal” couples (double-income couples, of which husbands do domestic labor a lot) have less children and earn higher income than other types of couples. Due to the Difference Principle, there is no reason to support them.Fourthly, I propose the Japanese government provides “child allowance” to all children under 18 years old equally. It is based not on the theory of the “child care free rider, ” but on the child's right to live. The present public nursery service gives priority to double-income couples. It is unfair because of the unequal accessibility to the service by the parents' lifestyles and income. If the public nursery service cannot solve such inequality, then it must be privatized.Finally, the financial costs of “child allowance” must be shared by all citizens over 30 years old. I suppose there are three options to generate these costs. The priority will be as follows : cutting a part of the pension plan for child allowance; increasing the consumption tax; and increasing the income tax. This political strategy will be able to solve the unequal freedom of choice under the present child care support system, and can improve the imbalance in benefits of and contributions to the pension system among generations.

records.title: GENDER DISCRIMINATION IN EDUCATION: WHAT MOTIVATES PARENTS TO INVEST MORE IN SONS?
records.abstract: Gender discrimination exists in many different forms, and in many different countries and contexts. A wide body of empirical evidence suggests the existence and persistence of gender discrimination within the household. Boys receive preferential treatment from parents in terms of health and educational inputs. In this paper I map out and examine the existence and extent of gender discrimination in India among school going children (ages 4-18) and compare outcomes based on different types of household heterogeneities, such as size, income, location etc. I use child-specific data on enrolment and educational expenditures incurred for all children in the household, thereby making comparison both within and across households. While the male bias exists in both the decision to enrol a child in school, and in the amount of money spent on their books, tuition etc, parents particularly favour first born children. Households in urban areas, and those that have fewer children tend to discriminate less in favour of boys. It also striking that as the number of children increases, parents have higher expectations of financial support in the future from their sons, suggesting that this expectation may be exacerbating the preferential treatment to boys.

records.title: Il Bonus Bebè del governo Renzi: quanto “bonus”?
records.venue: Institutional Research Information System University of Turin (University of Turin)
records.abstract: Renzi's Bonus Bebè: is it really "bonus"?With the approval of the new Stability Law at the end of 2014, Renzi Cabinet has introduced a new income transfer towards new parents with low resources -the so called "Bonus Bebè".Having a not too strict means-test and lasting for the first three years of the new child and not only around childbirth, this bonus represents a novelty in the Italian welfare tradition of familism by default.Yet, its selective nature and its modest amount are likely to limit its desired impact on fertility and poverty.Moreover, this new income transfer adds to the already existing fragmented measures in support to the cost of children on the one hand and to the poor on the other, without really strengthen and even less rationalize them.According to many scholars, in time of budget constraints and in front of a welfare system that still has to complete some crucial pillars, investing in more childcare services or in a unique general minimum income scheme would be a more appropriate route to follow. Keywords: child benefits -

records.title: Essays in the Economics of Education
records.abstract: This dissertation explores questions in financial aid, student loans, and homework time use. In chapter one, I use quarter of birth instruments to estimate the relationship between calculated financial need and actual financial aid received. A dollar increase in financial need is associated with 15 cents in federal grants and 47 cents in loans. However, the relationship between financial need and institutional aid is, on average, small and statistically insignificant. In chapter two, I use instrumental variables to estimate the effect of student loans on fertility later in life. First, I exploit a FAFSA loan-eligibility rule along with state-level variation in the school-entrance age to instrument for differences in loan availability. Next, I exploit state-by-SAT-score variation in tuition at public universities to instrument for differences in loan demand. I find that an increase in undergraduate loans, due to an increase in loan availability, does not significantly affect fertility. However, an increase in loans, due to higher tuition, decreases the number of children the student has 10 years after graduation. Back of the envelope calculations suggest that doubling tuition at in- state public colleges will lead to a 14 percent decrease in total fertility 10 years after graduation. In chapter three, we use the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) to document that Asian- American high-school students, on average, spend 2.3 times more time on homework compared to white students and 3.9 times more time on homework compared to black students. Our estimates suggest that the Asian-white homework gap is approximately 7.4 hours per week. Contrary to certain stereotypes, Asian-American students do not spend less time on leisure or sleep compared to white students. Rather, Asian-American students spending less time working for pay, doing household chores, and playing sports account for the entire Asian-white homework gap. We hypothesize that the differences in time use across ethnic groups may be related to the differences in educational outcomes across ethnic group

records.title: Financial Hardship in Settling Medical Bills among Households in a Semi-Urban Community in Northwest Nigeria Difficultées Financières à Honorer les Frais Médicaux pour des Ménages dans une Communauté Semi Urbaine au Nord-est du Nigeria
records.abstract: BACKGROUND: An equitable health care system that responds to the needs of its people is important to break the cycle of poverty and ill-health. However, rising health care cost, and the preponderance of user fees to finance health care have often limited access to needed health services. STUDY DESIGN: A cross-sectional descriptive study design was employed, using a pretested, semi-structured, intervieweradministered questionnaire. RESULTS: The study was carried out among 188 respondents. Majority (88.2%) of the respondents were within the agegroup 20-49 years, about two-thirds 63.8% were married and about half (42.8%) had family size between 5 and 9. The study revealed that about a quarter (26.1%) experienced hardship in settling their medical bills. While one-third (31.1%) had to sell their assets, about half (45.2%) had to secure loan while 16.6% had to resort to begging because of hardship encountered in settling the medical bills. Furthermore, of those who sold theirs asset; 46.2% sold their farmlands, 38.5% sold a piece of land, while 16.3% sold their vehicles. CONCLUSION: This study has revealed that inhabitants of Samaru community experience hardship in settling their medical bills. Consequently, innovative strategies like deferment of payment and fee exemption, enrolling into community-based health insurance schemes as well as voluntary contributory health insurance schemes etc need to be considered, in order to alleviate the hardship in settling the medical bills. WAJM 2013; 32(1): 14–18.

records.title: A survey of social, economic, and demographic causes for changes in rural fertility in Xianyang.
records.abstract: A study of intermediate variables affecting fertility in 3 rural villages and suburbs of Xianyang City, China was carried out to examine historical changes in household economy and socioeconomic factors from 1949-1987. Women in 151 households were surveyed in January-May 1988 on topics ranging from education status, marriage age, reproductive history, contraceptive history, occupation, to child-costs. Some data from a prior survey of 1000 married women in the province are also included. The marriage age was as low as 15 in older women, but 80% of women married at age 20-22 in 1985-87. The women had approximately 12% high school, 30% junior high school, 30% elementary school educated and 30% illiterate. Total fertility ranged from 4-8.5 in the 1940s-19509s, to 2.5 in the 1980s. Now most women prefer 2 children, although some want 3. Most wished for 1 son and 1 daughter. Neither education nor socioeconomic status affected sex preference. Costs and benefits of children, particularly the role of males in providing income for parents, were strong motivators. Analyses of costs of children showed that parents were very aware of the income derived from male children, but did not take into account the time spent raising children, nor did they realize the income girls bring in, a low but steady income while boys are still in school. Boys cost more to raise because of significantly higher expenses for 1st month celebration and marriages. Girls costs were higher for clothing, but they bring in money at marriage. In China today the actual fertility rate is higher than the expected because of male sex preference, problems with contraceptive supplies, and lack of awareness of the negative impact of social and economic policies on family planning.

records.title: Study on the Operation of Private Vocational Colleges in Taiwan
records.abstract: Along with the increase of income recently in Taiwan,people in Taiwan develop urgent demands for education,which contributes to the open of university.However,the increase of enrollment opportunity also induces the pressure in recruiting and operation to the universities.Vocational school are faced with severe challenges in recruiting and operation,due to,on the one hand,the entry of WTO and reducing birth rate in the island,and on the other hand, excess vocational colleges and schools.There are 159 vocational schools,and among them there are 97 secondary vocational schools.However,recently,the vacancy from insufficient enrollment which has increased by degrees couple with the inadequate registration rate of the fresher make the situation worse.Vocational schools,without funds support,have to run upon the tuition income and equity fund,but the prerequisite of doing this is that they can recruit enough students.As a result,vocational schools have to adapt proper strategies in recruitment and operation to form distinguishing training features.They should also try to train talents needed by enterprises and to attract more students so that they would not be washed out.The paper,first of all,introduces the motivation,purpose and approaches of the research, then the history of the development of vocational schools;it discusses on the basis of literature the educational and economic development of vocational schools,at last,it proposes strategies in recruitment and operation,and puts forward relevant suggestions and draws conclusion.

records.title: Status Quo of the Compulsory Education of Children of the Mobile Population in Shaanxi Province and Its Strategy
records.abstract: The number of children aged at compulsory education among the mobile population in Shaanxi has grown up to 200,200. These children are faced with difficulty to go to school, high tuition and poor learning conditions in private schools. This problem owes largely to the system of household register, standard of tuition, arrangement of educational resources, equal educational right and whatever. Since the matter of education of children of the mobile population concerns the future of our nation, measures must be taken to strengthen the governmental function and solve their actual problems to improve the present situation.

records.title: Expansion of Cost-effect Analysis of Children and Its Contribution to Demographic Transition in China
records.abstract: The paper analyzes the ratio of cost-effect of children within family and in society. It concludes that the difference in expected fertility level between family and society is the imbalanced cost of children within family and in society. Population policy in China changes the cost-effect of children within family,thus influences the decision of child-bearing within family.

records.title: Preschool Child Care Costs In The Cost Structure For A Child: Theoretical Analysis
records.abstract: Under modern conditions in a view of the necessity of the efficient money spending and of the monitoring of the estimation of the demographic policy efficiency to create the costs structure for a child classification is highly up to date. The aim of the article is to investigate the cost for a child and to assign the place of the spendings for preschool child care and character building within the costs for a child classification framework. To achieve the aim, we identified the child care performers and their functions. Then we examined the existed cost for a child classifications for each performer. A family is the most important one, that’s why the special emphasis was focused on its spendings. We specified possible approaches for estimating the costs for a child while a special emphasis on the spendings for child care and character building was laid. As a result, a functional classification that allows to specificate such spendings was chosen. To manage social and economic processes better, to develop the preschool institutions system and to develop more effective fertility and labour policies the more active investigation of the spendings for child care and the classification of such spendings are needed. Also to consider child care as labour is very important because this will allow to increase its reputation and the quality of life for families with children.

records.title: Historic growth rates vary widely across the primary care physician disciplines.
records.abstract: Nested within a 40-year trend of specialty-to-population growth outpacing that of primary care is variability in the rate of expansion within the different primary care disciplines. With continued population aging trends, low annual birth rate, and expected health insurance expansion, it is vital that physician workforce policy be aimed at meeting population needs to deliver optimal primary care.

records.title: Ghana's Family Planning Program: A Neglected Policy Initiative?
records.abstract: IntroductionThe world's population in 2002 was estimated to be 6.2 billion; expected to be growing by 75 million per annum, with 97 percent of this increase occurring in developing countries (Goldstein & Whitworth, 2005). A disproportionate share of developing countries' contribution to this rise is accounted for by the faster growth rate in Sub-Saharan African nations. This has raised fears of the inevitability of overpopulation in the sub region with its attendant negative consequences such as scarcity of productive resources, stress and strain on social infrastructure, environmental degradation etc. The concern about population size has also been expressed in Ghana over the years. The country's population increased from 6 million at independence in 1957 to nearly 18 million in 1996 with a projected estimate of 27 million by 2020 (Arjun, 1996; GMHS, 2007). With the current growth rate of 2.7 percent, the population may reach 32 million by 2040. The past rapid growth of Ghana's population was an outcome of high fertility, which until recently remained fairly constant, and declining mortality (Arjun, 1996; PPAG, 2009).Even though life expectancy at birth is low at 57.7 years and infant mortality is high at 71 per 1000 births (UNDP, 2007), this has not prevented the population from growing above the annual desirable rate. This has raised fears of an imminent overpopulation, with the government responding by introducing the Family Planning Program (FPP) in 1970. The FPP was strengthened by the launching of the Road Map for Repositioning Family Planning - 2006 to 2010 in 2006 (PPAG, 2009). Despite the fact that the FPP has been running for many years in Ghana it has failed to impact population in a meaningful way. The failure is attributed to factors such as dwindling government commitment in terms of advocacy and resourcing, gap between knowledge of family planning and use of contraceptives, unpredictability of donor funding, and high unmet need (PPAG, 2009; GMHS, 2007).Meanwhile, a seemingly conflicting initiative to the FPP, an exemptions policy for delivery fees for pregnant women was introduced in 2004 (MoH, 2004). This was gradually phased out and was replaced by health insurance in 2008 (popularly referred to as the Free Medical Care for Pregnant Women - FMCPW). The exemptions policy has an objective of addressing some of the challenges hindering the attainment of one of the Millennium Development Goals (MDG), which focuses on improving maternal health of women by 2015 (Osabutey, 2008). In other words, the policy is meant to curb the high rate of maternal and baby deaths.From the above exposition, it appears the FPP with its emphasis on limiting the number of children per woman, has an anti-natal intent (reducing fertility), while the FMCPW, which focuses on safe delivery, has a pro-natal motive. However, the government has prioritized the unacceptable level of maternal deaths as a national emergency and has diverted much attention and resources to dealing with the problem. The questions that then arise are: Has the prioritizing of the FMCPW left the FPP unattended to? What are the implications of this apparent neglect of the FPP for population growth and development of Ghana? These questions can be answered by providing responses to three further questions:1. Does Ghana need a Family Planning Program?2. Will the Family Planning Program reduce fertility?3. Is the FPP a neglected policy initiative?MethodologyData for the study was obtained from both primary and secondary sources. The primary information was obtained by interviewing 21 key personnel from relevant organizations including the Ghana Health Service, hospitals, and the Planned Parenthood Association of Ghana (PPAG). These respondents were originally identified because of their role connected directly to the development and implementation of the FPP and FMCPW policies. The secondary information was derived from content analysis of published works on both policy initiatives. …
